- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.

Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally reports a league-wide study, "under review" at the time of the talk, using public MLB data (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Window:** 2004 to 2014, chosen so that players who had surgery in 2014 had time to return (z_6M5r7031A [11:44] to [12:14]).
- **Counts:** about 200 surgeries, and on average 180 days of MLB-calendar time missed (z_6M5r7031A [12:14]). About half the players were starters and half relievers, with a small proportion of closers (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Total:** adjusted to 2017 levels, "half a billion dollars" of salary lost over the period to rehab alone (z_6M5r7031A [12:44]).
- **Excluded:** medical, travel and rehab costs; downtime before the surgery; lost team wins; trade value; and every minor league player (z_6M5r7031A [12:44] to [13:44]). He speculates the full cost might be 1 billion or 1.5 billion and says "I don't know" (z_6M5r7031A [13:44]).
- **Per player:** medical cost of about $50,000, which he calls conservative (z_6M5r7031A [11:13]). (Untested: bare assertion, no method given.)
- **Salary per WAR:** it "balloons" after surgery and does not return to the pre-surgery level until 3 years after the pitcher returns (z_6M5r7031A [10:43]). In Q&A he calls the salary-over-WAR calculation "relatively back of the envelope" and not adjusted (z_6M5r7031A [28:27]). (Untested: back-of-envelope, unadjusted.)

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism; this is an accounting of public salary data. Inference: it counts only direct salary during rehab, which is why the number is a floor on the speaker's own account.

**When to apply** — As an example of costing an injury type from public records by counting time missed and attaching a value. Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: a Baylor version would count games and practices missed by injury type and position group with Athletic Medicine, with no salary figure.

**When NOT to apply** — The study was under review, not published, at the time. Baylor athletes have no player salaries, so dollar figures and dollars per WAR do not transfer to college. The salary-per-WAR calculation is unadjusted and the speaker's own words are "back of the envelope." The 180-day figure is MLB calendar time. It is professional baseball pitchers only, and it counts surgeries, not all injuries.

**Example** — The speaker's own: about 200 surgeries over 2004 to 2014 and 180 MLB-calendar days missed on average, summing to half a billion 2017 dollars (z_6M5r7031A [12:14] to [12:44]).

Files docs/method-baseline.md and .claude/worktrees/step1-triage/docs/method-baseline.md differ
143:- No formal injury-risk model (ACWR, tissue-capacity tracking, a biomechanical screening protocol with defined red flags) is attributed to Eric anywhere in this corpus; the detailed treatment of ACWR and injury-risk modeling that does exist (Clemson curriculum) is reference material only, not confirmed Baylor practice. We've avoided them up to this point, but there's not a really good reason why." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q12)**
145:- Movement screens are collected and filed, not used to change programs. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12): "there isn't anything that changes decisions made to a program; it's more or less just collected and referred to for future needs." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q12)** Inference: this sits uneasily with his own Q3 rule; see Tension 15.

Injury risk: no formal model, ACWR distrusted, screens not acted on (Q12). Recovery and sleep: load design only, nothing objective tracked (Q23). Nutrition: no proactive data flow (Q24). Rehab and RTP: role stated (Q4, Q22) and a written protocol exists in the UE and LE templates (Q4a), not yet staged. Coaching stays thin: constraints-led coaching is not used (Q25), and the rest is unclaimed course material.

Yet ACWR is still looked at ("We dabble with ACWR") though he does not "trust it for anything", and movement screens are "just collected" without changing decisions (Q12). Inference: by his own rule both are candidates to retire or to be given a question.

=== claim--acwr-association-reproduced-when-acwr-has-no-effect.md

# In Simulated Seasons Where ACWR Does Nothing, It Still Predicts Injury About as Strongly as the Literature Reports

**What it is** — The speakers report that in their real NFL and Italian-soccer data, ACWR (last 7 days of load over last 28 days) is "highly predictive of injury in a particular session" (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:12]). They then simulated 1,000 seasons per sport in which injury probability depended only on the intensity of the current session, so ACWR had no effect by construction (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:43], [14:13]). In those simulations a chi-square test of ACWR against injury was "extremely highly significant" (TIRINmtZOu0 [14:43]). The apparent increase in injury risk was 6.8% for the Italian team and 10.5% for the NFL team, which the speaker says is "about of the same order" as effects reported across sports in the literature (TIRINmtZOu0 [15:15]). The talk does not say whether 6.8% and 10.5% are relative or absolute, and the numbers come from auto-captions and were not checked against the slides. They also say the first published paper, on cricket bowlers, appeared in 2014 and has been cited over 250 times, and that hundreds of papers followed (TIRINmtZOu0 [06:36], [07:07], [07:38]).

**Why it works** — The speakers' explanation is that a hard past week makes a hard session today likely, and today's intensity is what drives injury; see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]. The simulation itself is the evidence that the pattern can arise without any ACWR effect; the speakers do not show that it did arise that way in the published studies.

**When to apply** — When reading an ACWR injury paper or vendor claim: Inference: treat a reported ACWR effect of 5 to 10% as within what the schedule alone can produce in these two datasets. Inference: ask any vendor showing an ACWR risk curve whether it adjusts for the load of the session in which injury occurred. Eric's baseline: ACWR is looked at but not trusted for any decision, and there is no formal risk model (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit).

**When NOT to apply** — Two teams, two sports (NFL and a European club); no stated roster size, number of injuries or load variable, so do not read 6.8% and 10.5% as a college football estimate. The speakers say they have not disproved the field (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:49]); in Q&A, a speaker says a more multivariate model might still find signal (TIRINmtZOu0 [23:35]). A speaker's view (captions have no speaker labels) that the products are "snake oil" is stated opinion near the start of the talk (TIRINmtZOu0 [01:01]). The simulation reproduces the association's size, not its shape: the talk does not show that the U-shape or the sweet spot (captions "08 and 1.3", probably 0.8 to 1.3, TIRINmtZOu0 [05:36]) arises from the artifact.

**Example** — The speakers' own: NFL 10.5% and Italian soccer 6.8% apparent increase in risk from a null simulation (TIRINmtZOu0 [15:15]).

**Related** — [[framework--null-model-simulation-to-test-a-risk-metric]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]. Existing library, agrees in direction: [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]] (acute load alone and random-denominator ratios performed like ACWR in Serie A data). Existing library, the association literature: [[research-papers/griffin-2020-the-association-between-the-acute-chronic-workload-ratio-and-injury-and-its-application-in]].
=== claim--wellness-questionnaires-collapse-to-one-number.md

# Daily Wellness Questionnaires Often Collapse to the Same Number

**What it is** — In the Q&A, a speaker says the injury and training relationship is a dose and response relationship, and that, in the caption's words, "I don't think in team sport we have a great measure of response at the moment." Wellness questionnaires are "a good idea," but "I've never seen any good validation," and in "four different sports" over "years of data" the data are "essentially a bunch of professional athletes putting the number seven in every day" (TIRINmtZOu0 [24:39]). The caption says "seven"; the scale is not stated. The speaker is not identified in the captions between the two presenters.

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for why athletes enter one value. Inference: a repeated low-effort answer is the quickest way to finish a daily form, and nothing about the answer is checked against an outcome.

**When to apply** — As a check before putting a subjective wellness item into a multivariate injury or readiness model: look at the within-athlete variance first. Inference: if most athletes' entries barely move across weeks, the item cannot carry a signal. Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys rolled out across sports in summer 2022 were abandoned after about one academic year because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers, and wellness surveys are still used in return-to-play and chronic-health cases (Explicit, SportSmith piece, 2026-02-19). Inference: the speaker's observation matches Eric's reason for dropping them.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one speaker's experience across four sports, not a study, and no values, sample size or teams are given. It is not a statement that all subjective monitoring fails; a speaker (unclear if the same one) says that counting more things in a "more multivariate approach" might "tease out a meaningful signal" and that complex mechanisms may still predict injury (TIRINmtZOu0 [23:35], [24:06]); the captions do not name wellness data in that remark. Professional athletes are the stated population; a college roster with different incentives may behave differently.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the number "seven" entered every day by professional athletes, across four sports and years of data (TIRINmtZOu0 [24:39]).

**Related** — [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]] (the same Q&A, on whether richer data could replace the ratio). Existing library: [[research-papers/rebelo-2026-monitoring-training-effects-in-athletes-a-multidimensional-framework-for-decision-making]] (multidimensional monitoring).
=== framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load.md

# Adjust Injury Models for the Load of the Session Itself

**What it is** — The speakers' proposed fix is to include the actual load of the session in which an injury occurred, alongside any prior-load ratio (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]). Options they name: survival models, which look at when the athlete was injured and how intense the session was up to that moment; latent variable models that use the loads of other players in the same session who were not injured (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49], [18:19]); and, in the Q&A, predicting the upcoming session's load from the previous seven days and treating it as an unmeasured confounder (TIRINmtZOu0 [25:11]). They report that once session load was accounted for, ACWR went "from being highly significant to being non-significant" in all their cases (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19], [18:49]). They also report that acute load alone gave the same results as the ratio, and that coupled and uncoupled denominators gave the same results (TIRINmtZOu0 [26:42]).

**Why it works** — If session intensity is the confounder, holding it fixed removes the route through which the ratio looks predictive; see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]. The speakers do not show the models, the adjusted effect sizes, or the confidence intervals ("in the paper", TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]), so the mechanism is described, not demonstrated, in the talk.

**When to apply** — When building or auditing an injury model on load data with session-level records. Inference: a first pass is to compare a model with the prior-load ratio alone against the same model plus today's planned session load. In the Q&A a speaker notes the approach needs "a fair bit of statistical um chops" and that much of the original literature was brought up by "people whose background potentially is not very statistical" (TIRINmtZOu0 [25:11], [25:41]). Eric's baseline: there is no formal risk model, and sport science support exists for few teams ("we don't have sport science support for most teams", interview 2026-09-28, Q12 and Q28, Explicit). Inference: this would need dedicated analyst time.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested here: significance vanishing is reported, with no effect sizes, sample size, injury counts or model specification. Inference: significance loss says little about whether a real effect exists, since the talk gives no injury counts; the speakers say a richer multivariate model may still find a signal (TIRINmtZOu0 [23:35]). Requires session load for every player and session, including the injured one, which a speaker says is usually thrown out (see [[heuristic--keep-the-load-of-the-injured-session]]). Two teams, two sports.

**Example** — Inference: for a non-contact hamstring injury in a Tuesday practice, the record would hold the Tuesday session's planned intensity next to the prior-week ratio; the model asks whether the ratio adds anything once Tuesday's intensity is in.

**Related** — [[heuristic--keep-the-load-of-the-injured-session]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]; [[framework--null-model-simulation-to-test-a-risk-metric]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]].

The speaker then argues recovery is longer than 10 days (see the vulnerability-window entry) and reruns it at 60 days out: "21% of playing days", "one out of five athletes out at all times", about four of a football team's starters and one hockey starter at any moment, not counting repeat concussions (npgdKKdJSww [13:43], [14:14]). The speaker's conclusion is that either medical guidelines get much looser ("which won't happen") or the games change, starting with how much contact they contain (npgdKKdJSww [14:45], [22:58]).
-The speaker says the math was done "on the plane" and that "the science is iffy" on the 10-day figure (npgdKKdJSww [12:12]).

The model ignores repeat concussions, position differences and substitutions. It is a 2012 talk, and the speaker discloses a consultant role and a test-owner tie (npgdKKdJSww [00:30]).

Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.
254:12. **Daily mRSI testing against a Wednesday read.** The SportSmith piece describes mRSI from daily CMJ testing as the daily readiness marker [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]. Q2 names Wednesday as the day. Inference: daily collection with one weekly decision day would reconcile them, but Eric did not say which; worth one follow-up.

Inference: Q22 is scoped to RTP, so these probably do not conflict, but the RTP templates should be checked.

=== framework--null-model-simulation-to-test-a-risk-metric.md
confidence: supported
# Null-Model Simulation: Check Whether a Risk Metric Can Look Predictive When It Has No Effect

**What it is** — A way to test a monitoring metric before trusting it. The speakers (Luke Bourne, caption spelling, and Patrick Ward) built it for the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR). The steps as they describe them: (1) take real session-load data from a team, in their case one NFL team and one Italian soccer team (the captions say "Syria" and "Serria", probably Serie A, unconfirmed) (TIRINmtZOu0 [12:11]); (2) assume a "null model" in which everything leading into a session is irrelevant and only the intensity of the current session changes injury probability (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:12], [13:43]); (3) simulate whole seasons of injuries under that rule, 1,000 seasons per sport (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:43]); (4) run the same test the published studies run (a chi-square test of ACWR against injury) on the simulated seasons (TIRINmtZOu0 [14:13], [14:43]); (5) if the metric still "predicts" injury, the usual analysis cannot tell the metric's effect from the schedule's effect.

**Why it works** — The simulation fixes the true cause by construction, so any association between ACWR and injury that appears must come from how the data are structured, not from ACWR. The speakers' account of that structure is in [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]. The speakers do not describe the simulation code or how session loads were drawn; that detail is in their paper and was not shown (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]).

**When to apply** — Before adopting any ratio, rolling-window or flag as an injury-risk score, or when someone reports a clean association between a monitoring metric and injury. Inference: the same design can be run on a department's own load data, with the null set to "only the planned intensity of today's session matters," to see how much apparent signal the schedule alone manufactures. Eric's baseline: "We dabble with ACWR but I don't personally trust it for anything" and there is no formal risk model (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit). Eric's baseline: a test or technology that "doesn't answer a question anyone has" has no place (interview 2026-09-28, Q3, Explicit); this check is a cheap way to ask whether a flag answers one.

**When NOT to apply** — The talk reports the result for two teams in two sports, with no stated roster size, injury count or load metric, so the size of the artifact in a college football season is unknown. A simulation shows that an artifact is possible and of a certain size under the assumed null; it does not show the published studies are wrong, and the speakers say so (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:49]). It cannot be run without session-level load for every player, and the null (only today's intensity matters) is the speakers' assumption, not a measured fact. Single conference presentation; the adjusted analysis was not shown.

**Example** — The speakers' own: 1,000 simulated seasons per sport in which ACWR was irrelevant by design still produced an extremely significant chi-square result, and an apparent injury-risk increase of 6.8% (Italian team) and 10.5% (NFL team), figures read from auto captions (TIRINmtZOu0 [14:43], [15:15]). See [[claim--acwr-association-reproduced-when-acwr-has-no-effect]].

**Related** — [[claim--acwr-association-reproduced-when-acwr-has-no-effect]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]; [[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]] (a different artifact test, random denominators, on Serie A data); [[research-papers/menaspa-2017-are-rolling-averages-a-good-way-to-assess-training-load-for-injury-prevention]].
=== heuristic--keep-the-load-of-the-injured-session.md
confidence: contested
# Keep the Load Record of the Session in Which an Injury Occurs

**What it is** — The speaker (Luke Bourne, caption spelling; named because the introduction lists "Luke Bourne and Patrick Ward" as presenters, Patrick hands over with "turn it over to Luke" at [10:10], and this passage refers back to "what Patrick was saying before" at [16:47]) says earlier studies did not use same-session load for a simple reason: when a player is injured mid-session, that session's data is "censored" or thrown out. His example is that nobody is going to "carefully extract the GPS unit" in the middle of the field during an NFL practice (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:18], [17:49]). The result is that the analysis sees load before the injury session but not the intensity of the session itself, which is the variable the speakers argue matters most (see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]). The speaker says analyses "need to account for" the session load in that session (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]) and names survival models (how intense it was until the moment of injury) as one route (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19]). Inference: the heuristic is to make sure the injured session's load, or at minimum its planned intensity, is saved.

Contested: the sibling entry [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (TbYgc6_qQzo, Patrick Ward, [04:36], [12:15] to [12:47]) removes the injured-and-removed session from the data for that injury day, so the shortened session does not pull loads down, while this talk names that same removal ("censored, thrown out") as the reason earlier analyses missed same-session load. The two talks have the same presenters and are not reconciled in the captions. Treat the choice as open and state which rule a study used.

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is about missing data, not physiology: without the session's own load, a model cannot separate it from the prior-load ratio. The speaker gives no figure for how much data is lost. Inference: an injured athlete's device often stops mid-session, so the partial record can still carry the load up to the injury.

**When to apply** — Whenever the department logs injuries against GPS or session data. Eric's baseline: Catapult is the GPS stack, with a documented session lifecycle and data cleaning with spike detection (Explicit, Playbook p.7, pp.9-11). Inference: the cleaning step, or a missing export after an early stop, is the place where an injured session could be dropped; check that the partial session is retained and flagged. A practical first check: count how many non-contact injuries have a recorded session load for the day of injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the speaker's assertion about common practice in the literature, not a measured loss rate, and it comes from the NFL and European soccer. It does not by itself fix the confounding; the model adjustment is a separate step ([[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]). # Null-Model Simulation: Check Whether a Risk Metric Can Look Predictive When It Has No Effect

**What it is** — A way to test a monitoring metric before trusting it. The speakers (Luke Bourne, caption spelling, and Patrick Ward) built it for the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR). The steps as they describe them: (1) take real session-load data from a team, in their case one NFL team and one Italian soccer team (the captions say "Syria" and "Serria", probably Serie A, unconfirmed) (TIRINmtZOu0 [12:11]); (2) assume a "null model" in which everything leading into a session is irrelevant and only the intensity of the current session changes injury probability (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:12], [13:43]); (3) simulate whole seasons of injuries under that rule, 1,000 seasons per sport (TIRINmtZOu0 [13:43]); (4) run the same test the published studies run (a chi-square test of ACWR against injury) on the simulated seasons (TIRINmtZOu0 [14:13], [14:43]); (5) if the metric still "predicts" injury, the usual analysis cannot tell the metric's effect from the schedule's effect.

**Why it works** — The simulation fixes the true cause by construction, so any association between ACWR and injury that appears must come from how the data are structured, not from ACWR. The speakers' account of that structure is in [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]. The speakers do not describe the simulation code or how session loads were drawn; that detail is in their paper and was not shown (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]).

**When to apply** — Before adopting any ratio, rolling-window or flag as an injury-risk score, or when someone reports a clean association between a monitoring metric and injury. Inference: the same design can be run on a department's own load data, with the null set to "only the planned intensity of today's session matters," to see how much apparent signal the schedule alone manufactures. Eric's baseline: "We dabble with ACWR but I don't personally trust it for anything" and there is no formal risk model (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit). Eric's baseline: a test or technology that "doesn't answer a question anyone has" has no place (interview 2026-09-28, Q3, Explicit); this check is a cheap way to ask whether a flag answers one.

**When NOT to apply** — The talk reports the result for two teams in two sports, with no stated roster size, injury count or load metric, so the size of the artifact in a college football season is unknown. A simulation shows that an artifact is possible and of a certain size under the assumed null; it does not show the published studies are wrong, and the speakers say so (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:49]). It cannot be run without session-level load for every player, and the null (only today's intensity matters) is the speakers' assumption, not a measured fact. Single conference presentation; the adjusted analysis was not shown.

**Example** — The speakers' own: 1,000 simulated seasons per sport in which ACWR was irrelevant by design still produced an extremely significant chi-square result, and an apparent injury-risk increase of 6.8% (Italian team) and 10.5% (NFL team), figures read from auto captions (TIRINmtZOu0 [14:43], [15:15]). See [[claim--acwr-association-reproduced-when-acwr-has-no-effect]].

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

# The Training Schedule Can Create an ACWR to Injury Association Without ACWR Causing Injury

**What it is** — The speakers (Luke Bourne, caption spelling, and Patrick Ward) propose a causal structure, drawn as a directed acyclic graph (TIRINmtZOu0 [11:10]). The published analyses compute ACWR going into each session and check whether an injury occurred in that session (TIRINmtZOu0 [10:10], [10:40]). The speakers add a missing third variable: the schedule drives both ACWR and the intensity of the upcoming session, and session intensity drives injury (TIRINmtZOu0 [11:10], [11:41]). If the last seven days were hard, ACWR is high, and the next session is also likely to be hard (TIRINmtZOu0 [11:41]). Their density plots show that when athletes are in the "danger zone" of ACWR, upcoming session loads are higher than when they are in the "sweet spot" (TIRINmtZOu0 [16:16], [16:47]). Schedule features named: training camp, where load jumps from zero to a lot, international breaks, and the weekly cycle (TIRINmtZOu0 [09:39], [16:47], [17:18]). They open with an ice cream and drowning example of confounding (TIRINmtZOu0 [03:33]).

**Why it works** — The structure is a standard confounder: a shared cause makes two variables move together. The speakers show two things: the simulation in [[claim--acwr-association-reproduced-when-acwr-has-no-effect]], and that in their real data the ACWR association goes from "highly significant to non-significant" once same-session load is accounted for, in all their cases (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19], [18:49]). The adjusted effect sizes and models are "in the paper" and were not shown (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]). The speakers give no physiological mechanism for why session intensity raises injury risk; they treat it as given. Inference: a high-intensity session in itself being the injury exposure is consistent with how they frame it, but the talk does not test it.

**When to apply** — Whenever a load metric computed from the days before a session is correlated with an outcome in that session. Inference: check whether the metric also predicts the load of the session itself; if it does, the metric may be a proxy for that load. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue." (Inferred (transcript), HHPR 5355 class 1). Inference: the talk does not contradict this: it says the ratio may reflect the schedule and leaves open whether spikes themselves cause injury.

**When NOT to apply** — Contested. This is the speakers' explanation, supported by one simulation and unshown real-data adjustments from two teams. The speakers themselves say they have not disproved the earlier papers and that the explanation is "another really good explanation" (TIRINmtZOu0 [19:19]). Existing library: Griffin 2020, a systematic review of 22 studies, reports ACWR associations with non-contact injury and recommends use inside a broader multifactorial monitoring system, so it does not read the association as pure artifact; Impellizzeri 2020 agrees with the artifact reading on Serie A data. Whether chronic load is protective is explicitly not addressed, in the speaker's Q&A answer (TIRINmtZOu0 [26:11], [26:42]). Do not use this entry to claim that training load is irrelevant to injury.

**Example** — The speakers' own: training camp, where coaches "purposefully increase training demands" and where the literature also finds the highest injury risk, raises ACWR and session intensity together (TIRINmtZOu0 [09:39]).

**Related** — [[framework--null-model-simulation-to-test-a-risk-metric]]; [[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]; [[claim--acwr-association-reproduced-when-acwr-has-no-effect]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-acute-to-random-workload-ratio-is-as-associated-with-injury-as-acute-to-actual-chronic-wor]] (agrees); [[research-papers/griffin-2020-the-association-between-the-acute-chronic-workload-ratio-and-injury-and-its-application-in]] (the association literature, disagrees in emphasis); [[research-papers/impellizzeri-2020-training-load-and-injury-part-2-questionable-research-practices-hijack-the-truth-and-misle]].

# Keep the Load Record of the Session in Which an Injury Occurs

**What it is** — The speaker (Luke Bourne, caption spelling; named because the introduction lists "Luke Bourne and Patrick Ward" as presenters, Patrick hands over with "turn it over to Luke" at [10:10], and this passage refers back to "what Patrick was saying before" at [16:47]) says earlier studies did not use same-session load for a simple reason: when a player is injured mid-session, that session's data is "censored" or thrown out. His example is that nobody is going to "carefully extract the GPS unit" in the middle of the field during an NFL practice (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:18], [17:49]). The result is that the analysis sees load before the injury session but not the intensity of the session itself, which is the variable the speakers argue matters most (see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]). The speaker says analyses "need to account for" the session load in that session (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]) and names survival models (how intense it was until the moment of injury) as one route (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19]). Inference: the heuristic is to make sure the injured session's load, or at minimum its planned intensity, is saved.

Contested: the sibling entry [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (TbYgc6_qQzo, Patrick Ward, [04:36], [12:15] to [12:47]) removes the injured-and-removed session from the data for that injury day, so the shortened session does not pull loads down, while this talk names that same removal ("censored, thrown out") as the reason earlier analyses missed same-session load. The two talks have the same presenters and are not reconciled in the captions. Treat the choice as open and state which rule a study used.

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is about missing data, not physiology: without the session's own load, a model cannot separate it from the prior-load ratio. The speaker gives no figure for how much data is lost. Inference: an injured athlete's device often stops mid-session, so the partial record can still carry the load up to the injury.

**When to apply** — Whenever the department logs injuries against GPS or session data. Eric's baseline: Catapult is the GPS stack, with a documented session lifecycle and data cleaning with spike detection (Explicit, Playbook p.7, pp.9-11). Inference: the cleaning step, or a missing export after an early stop, is the place where an injured session could be dropped; check that the partial session is retained and flagged. A practical first check: count how many non-contact injuries have a recorded session load for the day of injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the speaker's assertion about common practice in the literature, not a measured loss rate, and it comes from the NFL and European soccer. It does not by itself fix the confounding; the model adjustment is a separate step ([[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]). Contact injuries are outside the speakers' definition, which is a non-contact injury that makes the player miss a subsequent session or match, in line with the UEFA definition (TIRINmtZOu0 [20:22], [20:53]); the speaker also says an off-field injury cannot be ruled out as training-related (TIRINmtZOu0 [20:22]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a player injured in the middle of an NFL practice, where "the last thing they're worried about" is capturing the GPS data (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]).

confidence: supported
# 101 Football Athletes, One Season: Volume and Impacts Tracked Non-Contact Injury

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") and co-authors analyzed one full season, preseason through regular season, in 101 American football athletes (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:14]). The aim was not to predict injuries before a session but to identify the relationship between training-load variables and non-contact time-loss injury, so practitioners get an idea of associated risk (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]).

- **Metrics from inertial sensor units** (vendor not named in the transcript): total player load, four player load effort bands, impacts with three thresholds, and inertial movement analysis (IMA) with three thresholds (TbYgc6_qQzo [08:12] to [09:12]).
- **Injuries:** 29 non-contact time-loss injuries, mostly lower extremity, plus an oblique in a linebacker, a low back strain and an elbow strain in a defensive lineman who was learning a new position (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:18] to [13:49]).
- **Models:** the best model within each metric group, then a joint model. The player load model used total player load and player load "very high"; the IMA and impacts models used all three bands; the joint model used total player load, player load low and impacts high and was "the most useful" for explaining injury (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:49] to [14:20]).
- **Direction of effects:** total player load and impacts high carried the highest increase in risk; player load low had a decreased association (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:20] to [15:22]). Ward reads total player load as volume and impacts high as session intensity or physicality, interesting because collision injuries were not studied (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:51]).
- **Position group:** adding it as a categorical variable did not help in any model, and the speaker suspects too few injuries per group (TbYgc6_qQzo [15:22] to [15:53]).
- **Timing:** in Q&A, most injuries occurred in training camp, very few once the season started (TbYgc6_qQzo [22:05]).
- **Not shown:** effect sizes, thresholds or band values (the transcript gives none), and no game load (TbYgc6_qQzo [16:53]).

**Why it works** — Ward's interpretation for the inverse player-load-low result is that a session cannot be high and low intensity at the same time, so the inverse relation is "logical" (TbYgc6_qQzo [15:22]). The speaker gives no mechanism for why impacts would raise non-contact risk. Inference: it may reflect session physicality or camp-style practice, but the talk does not say.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a template for which Catapult columns to read beside the standard load view after practice (total volume, a high-intensity impacts count, and the low band) instead of one load number. Eric's baseline: core GPS metrics tracked include player load, field time and IMA for indoor sessions (Explicit, Playbook pp.11-13). Eric's baseline: no sport- or position-specific GPS thresholds exist formally ("They do not exist formally," Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q7). Inference: this study supplies no thresholds to fill that gap. Inference: camp weeks, where most injuries fell here, are where a Baylor descriptive look would start.

**When NOT to apply** — One team, one season, 29 injuries, and no effect sizes. The talk does not name the team or level; a questioner refers to roster reduction to "a final 53" (TbYgc6_qQzo [21:35]), which suggests an NFL-style roster, but that is not confirmed. Association only, with no game load. Injury types were pooled across hamstring, adductor and other injuries (TbYgc6_qQzo [16:23] to [16:53]). Do not set a Baylor load limit from it, and do not change practice plans because one session scored high on impacts. Ward says thresholds "bounce around" between studies (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:06]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: the defensive lineman's elbow extensor strain came while learning a new position and doing exercises unique to him in training (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (how the data were coded). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]]. [[claim--ima-informs-linemen-where-gps-distance-does-not]].

# Inertial Movement Analysis May Describe Linemen Where GPS Distance Does Not

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") defines inertial movement analysis (IMA) as a count of movements in different directions (forward, backward, right, left and in between), built from accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer data and reported in three threshold bands (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:12]). His argument: GPS-type measures say a lot about outside players such as defensive backs and wide receivers, who produce much locomotor activity, but little about offensive and defensive linemen, because reliability falls when units record high-intensity activity in small spaces, "say below 20 meters," which is what linemen do (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:44]). The speaker says "we think this may be a useful metric" (TbYgc6_qQzo [09:44]).

Support offered, all described verbally without data: earlier work showing the metrics differentiate position groups in running and non-running activity, and proof-of-concept examples: a wide receiver running a straight sprint and a cut, the 5-10-5 pro agility drill, and a sled hit and drive-through (TbYgc6_qQzo [10:14] to [11:14]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the unit-reliability point above. The talk gives no figures for reliability by distance or for how IMA performs for linemen.

**When to apply** — Inference: when reporting offensive and defensive line sessions, where total distance may under-describe the work. Eric's baseline: IMA is among the core GPS metrics tracked, used for indoor sessions without GPS coverage (Explicit, Playbook pp.11-13). Inference: this talk proposes a different use for the same metric, small-space line work, which the baseline does not state.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: no data are shown for the linemen claim, and the examples are single-athlete drills. The 20-meter reliability point is the speaker's statement with no citation. IMA band thresholds are not given. In the injury study, IMA models were fit but the joint model did not retain IMA, and no position-group effect was found, so the study does not show IMA helps for linemen (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:20], [15:22]).

**Example** — The speaker's own list of proof-of-concept exercises includes a collision-based sled hit and drive-through, alongside the 5-10-5 (TbYgc6_qQzo [10:44] to [11:14]). The transcript does not report what IMA showed for any of them.

**Related** — [[case-study--101-football-athletes-one-season-load-and-non-contact-injury]] (the study in which IMA was one metric group).

# "No Research Links Joint Range or Posture to Injury": Said in the Q&A, Disputed by the Questioner

**What it is** — In Q&A an audience member said a full picture of injury risk needs internal load (heart rate load, time in zone), heart rate variability and recovery profiles, hydration, hip mobility asymmetry and pain and soreness, plus RPE (TbYgc6_qQzo [19:27] to [19:59]); the captions carry no speaker labels, so the split between questioner and presenter in that run of words is a reading, not certain. The next sentence, that the number of teams collecting all that data is "pretty much zero," cannot be attributed to either voice. The speaker's reply says "we collect all that data" but disagrees on the hip mobility piece, saying that while it "might be important," no research has been able to suggest that specific joint ranges of motion or even postures lead to injury or pain, and that you can find correlations in papers that look retrospectively (TbYgc6_qQzo [19:59] to [20:29]). The speaker added that a preseason mobility or posture measure will change as athletes adapt or are given a training intervention, so it would need re-measuring every week, which is possible but hard with about 120 athletes on a collegiate team (TbYgc6_qQzo [20:29] to [20:59]). The speaker agreed the full data would be "really helpful" (TbYgc6_qQzo [20:59]).

The audience member holds that hip mobility asymmetry belongs in the picture; the speaker says no research supports a link. The speaker partly concedes ("might be important") and the exchange is not resolved with data. Inference: the vault note on asymmetries and injury risk (below) may conflict, but it was not compared.

**Why it works** — The speaker's stated reason is that retrospective correlations differ from prediction and that measures taken in preseason go stale as athletes adapt (TbYgc6_qQzo [20:29]). The speaker cites no study for the blanket statement. Inference: "no research has ever" is a strong universal claim made aloud in Q&A and should not be cited as a literature finding.

**When to apply** — As a reason to ask what decision a mobility or posture screen changes before collecting it weekly. Eric's baseline: movement screens are "just collected and referred to for future needs" and change no program decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Eric's baseline: a test that "doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need" has no place (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q3). Inference: this exchange supports Eric's own caution about screens, and by his Q3 rule the screens are candidates to retire or to be given a question.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the claim is a universal negative asserted aloud with no citation, and the questioner's view was not rebutted with data. Do not cite it as proof that mobility or posture is irrelevant to injury, or as a reason to stop screening in rehab or return-to-play contexts, which the talk does not address. Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[afonso-undated-asymmetries-and-injury-risk-when-titles-spin-the-tale]], on asymmetry and injury risk, was not compared in this batch.

**Example** — The speaker's own point: an athlete's hip range measured in preseason and then changed by training means a single preseason value no longer describes him by midseason (TbYgc6_qQzo [20:29]).

**Related** — [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]] (the speaker's wider multifactorial view, which includes intrinsic factors).

# Single-Club Load Models Predicted Injury Poorly on Unseen Data

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") cites a tweet by "Luke borne" (caption spelling), whom the speaker calls "one of the co-authors on this paper" (the paper the tweet linked, by the captions), saying the sports science industry states "we predict injuries" while the research community says injury prediction is hard and unresolved (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39]). The tweet linked a paper from "David Carey's group out of Australia" (caption spelling). Ward's account of it: the group built predictive models of training load and injury in Australian football, tested them on unseen data, and concluded that models built from a single club's load data showed poor ability to predict injuries on previously unseen data, so they are limited as daily decision tools for practitioners (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39] to [07:10]). No accuracy figures are given in the talk.

Ward adds a contrast: technology companies tell practitioners to "dump your data in" and injury will be predicted, while the people collecting the data know how hard it is to get it clean and coded properly, and injury is multifactorial (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:10]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond injury being multifactorial and data quality being hard (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:10]). Inference: a model fit on one club's data may be capturing that club's practices and noise, which would fail on new data, but the talk does not say this.

**When to apply** — As the standard to ask of any vendor or paper claiming prediction: was it tested on unseen data, and at more than one club? Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is followed, and ACWR is looked at but not trusted (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: this is outside support for that decision to avoid formal models.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is a second-hand, uncited study (no authors' figures, sample or accuracy are given) relayed from a slide. It is Ward's secondhand description of one Australian football study, not a first-hand reading of it. The sport (Australian football) and the data source (single club) bound it; the talk does not say it holds for multi-club data or for American football. It is a statement about daily decision tools, not about whether load relates to injury at all; Ward's own study reports associations (see the case-study entry).

**Example** — The speaker's own: the sports science industry says "we predict injuries," the research community says it is hard, and the cited Australian group's out-of-sample test supports the research community (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39] to [07:10]).

**Related** — [[framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers]] (check 6). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[carey-2017-predictive-modelling-of-training-loads-and-injury-in-australian-football]] in the research-paper library; its title matches the paper Ward describes, but this batch did not open it, so verify they are the same study.
