=== framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers.md
confidence: untested
# A Checklist for Reading Training-Load and Injury Papers

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") opens his research-competition talk with the limits he sees in the published load and injury literature, from soccer and cricket to rugby and Australian football (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33]). Six checks, each with his stated reason:
1. **Contact versus non-contact.** Some papers code injury as a binary, injured in the session or game or not. Then the reader cannot tell whether load had anything to do with it or whether a player rolled up on another's leg (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33] to [04:04]).
2. **Time loss versus non-time loss.** Without it, severity is unknown. Time-loss injuries are the ones that keep players out (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:04]).
3. **Censoring.** If an athlete is hurt a quarter of the way into a session and removed, and the model does not censor that session, it can produce "really low training loads lead to high amounts of injuries" (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]).
4. **Thresholds.** Papers often end with a "train above X load, Y more injuries" rule, but thresholds "bounce around" between papers, even in one sport, because the samples are small, one team and one to two years of data (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:06]).
5. **Team-specific results.** The speaker says these papers are often less about predicting injury for a sport and more about one team and how its coach prepares it, comparing it to inconsistent coffee-and-wine nutrition headlines (TbYgc6_qQzo [05:37]).
6. **Retrospective versus predictive.** Papers say "prediction" in the title, but the model is never tested on unseen data; they are historical accounts of how injuries took place, which, the caption says, "isn't necessarily bad" (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:08]; the caption writes "retro addictive" for retrospective).

**Why it works** — Each check is paired with the failure it prevents, as listed above. The speaker gives no evidence on how often each failure occurs in the literature; he describes them as "some of the papers" (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33]). Inference: the checks work as a quick screen because each one changes what the reader can conclude (association versus prediction, one team versus a sport).

**When to apply** — Before acting on a published load-injury result or a vendor claim that load data predicts injury. Eric's baseline: Eric looks at ACWR but does not trust it for anything, calling it "raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally," and follows no formal risk model (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: this checklist gives specific reasons for that distrust, such as no unseen-data test and unstable thresholds.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is one researcher's critique, not a validated appraisal tool, and it gives no scoring or cut-off. It is not a replacement for a formal risk-of-bias instrument. It says nothing about the quality of the speaker's own study beyond what he states; see the case-study entry for that.

**Example** — The speaker's own, for check 3: an unadjusted model that kicks out "really low training loads lead to high amounts of injuries" because injured athletes' short sessions are left in (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]).

**Related** — [[claim--single-club-injury-models-predict-poorly-on-unseen-data]] (check 6 in practice). [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (how the speaker's own study handled checks 1 to 3). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]]. Reciprocal-link suggestions (not compared in this batch): [[impellizzeri-2020-training-load-and-injury-part-2-questionable-research-practices-hijack-the-truth-and-misle]], [[griffin-2020-the-association-between-the-acute-chronic-workload-ratio-and-injury-and-its-application-in]].
=== framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis.md
confidence: untested
# How the Study Coded Injuries, Scaled Load and Censored Sessions

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") describes how the one-season football study handled the limitations listed in other papers (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]):
1. **Injury definition:** any injury not due to contact with another player that results in the player missing subsequent training sessions or games, "really stringent" so only non-contact time-loss injuries counted (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:14] to [11:45]).
2. **Who coded:** a medical professional present at the diagnoses coded the injuries in a bespoke injury database (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:45]).
3. **Load scaling:** load variables normalized to session minutes (the density of the session), then standardized within each position group, to "borrow some strength" from position-group data because groups have different tasks (TbYgc6_qQzo [11:45] to [12:15]).
4. **Censoring:** an athlete who was injured in a session, evaluated by a medical professional and deemed unable to continue was removed from the data for that injury day, so the shortened session would not pull the data down (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:15] to [12:47]).
5. **Models:** logistic regression models, fit iteratively, with the caption reading "for" (read as four: one per load-variable family, player load, effort bands, impacts, IMA, TbYgc6_qQzo [08:12] to [09:12]) separate models plus a joint model (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:47]). Compared with the Bayesian information criterion and out-of-sample likelihood (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:47] to [13:18]).
6. **Out-of-sample check:** with too little data for a hold-out group, they used "a concept like leave one out cross validation" across the season (TbYgc6_qQzo [13:18]).

**Why it works** — Step 4 answers the problem named earlier, that without censoring a model can show low loads leading to injuries (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]). Step 1 and 2 answer the contact and severity problem (TbYgc6_qQzo [03:33] to [04:04]). The speaker gives no reason for position standardization beyond borrowing strength and position-specific tasks (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:15]).

**When to apply** — As a template for agreeing, between Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance, one injury definition and one rule for sessions where an athlete is injured, before any load analysis. Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-20, NordBord). Inference: consistent injury coding is the same kind of precondition. Eric's baseline: no sport- or position-specific GPS thresholds exist formally (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q7). Inference: the speaker's within-position standardization is one way to get position-specific load measures without published thresholds, though the speaker gives no thresholds.

**When NOT to apply** — The out-of-sample check is leave-one-out style within one team's one season, which is not an independent test; the speaker calls it "a concept like" that method. Band thresholds for effort bands and IMA are fixed but their values are not given (TbYgc6_qQzo [08:42] to [09:12]). Adding position group as a categorical predictor did not improve any model (29 injuries in the season, TbYgc6_qQzo [13:18], [15:22]). Confidence is untested because this entry describes a procedure; the results it produced are in [[case-study--101-football-athletes-one-season-load-and-non-contact-injury]]. The talk reports no inter-rater check on the injury coding.

**Example** — The speaker's own scenario: an athlete injured and removed early in a session (caption, garbled: "completes maybe of the first quarter of a session") should be censored, not kept in the data with a tiny load (TbYgc6_qQzo [04:36]). The rule applied in the study is step 4 above (TbYgc6_qQzo [12:15] to [12:47]).

**Related** — [[framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers]]. [[case-study--101-football-athletes-one-season-load-and-non-contact-injury]].
=== principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction.md
confidence: untested
# Training Load Gives Risk Context, Not Injury Prediction

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") frames the result as associated risk that practitioners can use "to build appropriate training sessions that are logical and hopefully mitigate injury," not as prediction before a session (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]). The speaker says practitioners can combine volume and intensity findings with the heuristics they have built over years of designing sessions (TbYgc6_qQzo [16:23]). To make a model truly predictive the speaker says it would need much more than load: "we're probably really naive" to think only load factors raise non-contact injury risk; there are intrinsic factors the athlete brings, extrinsic factors of the session, their interactions, and how those interactions change as players adapt or maladapt across a season (TbYgc6_qQzo [17:24] to [17:54]).

Q&A adds two cautions. An audience member argued that training is "endogenous to effort," so correlations could reflect players who try hard in both practice and games, and that random assignment would address it; the speaker agreed it would help if a coach would allow it, and noted the group also tracks perceived effort but did not use it in this paper (TbYgc6_qQzo [18:24] to [19:27]). Underreporting of pain by athletes is, the speaker says, one of the most complex limits in collegiate and professional sport (TbYgc6_qQzo [24:10]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's argument is multifactorial causation, as above. The speaker gives no data that other factors would improve prediction; that is a position, not a result. Inference: treating load as one risk input fits that position and avoids implying a certainty the model lacks.

**When to apply** — When a load report is used in a conversation with coaches about a practice plan. Eric's baseline: "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q6). Eric's baseline: "Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine" (Inferred (transcript), HHPR 5355 course material). Inference: both fit Ward's stance that a load measure informs the coach's judgment rather than replacing it.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is the speaker's stance, supported by the limits of the speaker's own study (29 injuries, one team, one season) but not tested as a decision approach. It gives no rule for how much weight to give load against other information. The endogeneity concern was raised by an audience member and only partly answered. Eric's baseline: no formal risk model is followed (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: that makes this principle a description of current practice, not a new method for Baylor.

**Example** — The speaker's own: impacts high is associated with higher non-contact risk, and practitioners can combine such findings with their own heuristics when building sessions (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:51], [16:23]). Inference: a high-impact session is a risk factor to weigh, not a signal to cancel work.

**Related** — [[case-study--101-football-athletes-one-season-load-and-non-contact-injury]]. [[claim--single-club-injury-models-predict-poorly-on-unseen-data]]. [[framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers]].
66:- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for smaller-framed lifters. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q10)**: no sport tests true 1RM now; was Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
67:- Velocity-based 1RM estimation (linear-displacement transducer, ~10% load increments to 85-90% or a target mean velocity) is preferred over live 1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing, with published target mean velocities at 1RM (squat 0.3 m/s, bench 0.2 m/s, power hang snatch 1.0 m/s, power hang clean 0.8 m/s). **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8, Q10)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md] Inference: Q10 describes projection from observation and history and does not mention a velocity protocol.
68:- The Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen, anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather than testing every sport the same way. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q9)**; was Inferred. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q9): "That assessment schedule was never used." Inference: the table was never practice, not just outdated. [update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md]
78:- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
85:- Core GPS metrics tracked: maximum velocity, total distance, player load, field time, heart-rate bands, velocity/acceleration/deceleration effort bands, and Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) for indoor sessions without GPS coverage. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.11-13, Data Dictionary]

# Keep the Load Record of the Session in Which an Injury Occurs

**What it is** — The speaker (Luke Bourne, caption spelling; named because the introduction lists "Luke Bourne and Patrick Ward" as presenters, Patrick hands over with "turn it over to Luke" at [10:10], and this passage refers back to "what Patrick was saying before" at [16:47]) says earlier studies did not use same-session load for a simple reason: when a player is injured mid-session, that session's data is "censored" or thrown out. His example is that nobody is going to "carefully extract the GPS unit" in the middle of the field during an NFL practice (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:18], [17:49]). The result is that the analysis sees load before the injury session but not the intensity of the session itself, which is the variable the speakers argue matters most (see [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]]). The speaker says analyses "need to account for" the session load in that session (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]) and names survival models (how intense it was until the moment of injury) as one route (TIRINmtZOu0 [18:19]). Inference: the heuristic is to make sure the injured session's load, or at minimum its planned intensity, is saved.

Contested: the sibling entry [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (TbYgc6_qQzo, Patrick Ward, [04:36], [12:15] to [12:47]) removes the injured-and-removed session from the data for that injury day, so the shortened session does not pull loads down, while this talk names that same removal ("censored, thrown out") as the reason earlier analyses missed same-session load. The two talks have the same presenters and are not reconciled in the captions. Treat the choice as open and state which rule a study used.

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is about missing data, not physiology: without the session's own load, a model cannot separate it from the prior-load ratio. The speaker gives no figure for how much data is lost. Inference: an injured athlete's device often stops mid-session, so the partial record can still carry the load up to the injury.

**When to apply** — Whenever the department logs injuries against GPS or session data. Eric's baseline: Catapult is the GPS stack, with a documented session lifecycle and data cleaning with spike detection (Explicit, Playbook p.7, pp.9-11). Inference: the cleaning step, or a missing export after an early stop, is the place where an injured session could be dropped; check that the partial session is retained and flagged. A practical first check: count how many non-contact injuries have a recorded session load for the day of injury.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the speaker's assertion about common practice in the literature, not a measured loss rate, and it comes from the NFL and European soccer. It does not by itself fix the confounding; the model adjustment is a separate step ([[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]). Contact injuries are outside the speakers' definition, which is a non-contact injury that makes the player miss a subsequent session or match, in line with the UEFA definition (TIRINmtZOu0 [20:22], [20:53]); in the Q&A, the presenter who answers (after the question is handed to the other presenter at [19:52]; not identified by name in the captions) also says an off-field injury cannot be ruled out as training-related (TIRINmtZOu0 [20:22]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a player injured in the middle of an NFL practice, where "the last thing they're worried about" is capturing the GPS data (TIRINmtZOu0 [17:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-coding-and-censoring-rules-for-load-analysis]] (conflicts: censors the injured session; TbYgc6_qQzo); [[framework--adjust-injury-models-for-same-session-load]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]].

# Training Load Gives Risk Context, Not Injury Prediction

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") frames the result as associated risk that practitioners can use "to build appropriate training sessions that are logical and hopefully mitigate injury," not as prediction before a session (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:41]). The speaker says practitioners can combine volume and intensity findings with the heuristics they have built over years of designing sessions (TbYgc6_qQzo [16:23]). To make a model truly predictive the speaker says it would need much more than load: "we're probably really naive" to think only load factors raise non-contact injury risk; there are intrinsic factors the athlete brings, extrinsic factors of the session, their interactions, and how those interactions change as players adapt or maladapt across a season (TbYgc6_qQzo [17:24] to [17:54]).

Q&A adds two cautions. An audience member argued that training is "endogenous to effort," so correlations could reflect players who try hard in both practice and games, and that random assignment would address it; the speaker agreed it would help if a coach would allow it, and noted the group also tracks perceived effort but did not use it in this paper (TbYgc6_qQzo [18:24] to [19:27]). Underreporting of pain by athletes is, the speaker says, one of the most complex limits in collegiate and professional sport (TbYgc6_qQzo [24:10]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's argument is multifactorial causation, as above. The speaker gives no data that other factors would improve prediction; that is a position, not a result. Inference: treating load as one risk input fits that position and avoids implying a certainty the model lacks.

**When to apply** — When a load report is used in a conversation with coaches about a practice plan. Eric's baseline: "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q6). Eric's baseline: "Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine" (Inferred (transcript), HHPR 5355 course material). Inference: both fit Ward's stance that a load measure informs the coach's judgment rather than replacing it.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is the speaker's stance, supported by the limits of the speaker's own study (29 injuries, one team, one season) but not tested as a decision approach. It gives no rule for how much weight to give load against other information. The endogeneity concern was raised by an audience member and only partly answered. Eric's baseline: no formal risk model is followed (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: that makes this principle a description of current practice, not a new method for Baylor.

**Example** — The speaker's own: impacts high is associated with higher non-contact risk, and practitioners can combine such findings with their own heuristics when building sessions (TbYgc6_qQzo [14:51], [16:23]). Inference: a high-impact session is a risk factor to weigh, not a signal to cancel work.

**Related** — [[case-study--101-football-athletes-one-season-load-and-non-contact-injury]]. [[claim--single-club-injury-models-predict-poorly-on-unseen-data]]. [[framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers]].

# Single-Club Load Models Predicted Injury Poorly on Unseen Data

**What it is** — Patrick Ward (caption spelling "Patrick ward") cites a tweet by "Luke borne" (caption spelling), whom the speaker calls "one of the co-authors on this paper" (the paper the tweet linked, by the captions), saying the sports science industry states "we predict injuries" while the research community says injury prediction is hard and unresolved (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39]). The tweet linked a paper from "David Carey's group out of Australia" (caption spelling). Ward's account of it: the group built predictive models of training load and injury in Australian football, tested them on unseen data, and concluded that models built from a single club's load data showed poor ability to predict injuries on previously unseen data, so they are limited as daily decision tools for practitioners (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39] to [07:10]). No accuracy figures are given in the talk.

Ward adds a contrast: technology companies tell practitioners to "dump your data in" and injury will be predicted, while the people collecting the data know how hard it is to get it clean and coded properly, and injury is multifactorial (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:10]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond injury being multifactorial and data quality being hard (TbYgc6_qQzo [07:10]). Inference: a model fit on one club's data may be capturing that club's practices and noise, which would fail on new data, but the talk does not say this.

**When to apply** — As the standard to ask of any vendor or paper claiming prediction: was it tested on unseen data, and at more than one club? Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is followed, and ACWR is looked at but not trusted (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: this is outside support for that decision to avoid formal models.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is a second-hand, uncited study (no authors' figures, sample or accuracy are given) relayed from a slide. It is Ward's secondhand description of one Australian football study, not a first-hand reading of it. The sport (Australian football) and the data source (single club) bound it; the talk does not say it holds for multi-club data or for American football. It is a statement about daily decision tools, not about whether load relates to injury at all; Ward's own study reports associations (see the case-study entry).

**Example** — The speaker's own: the sports science industry says "we predict injuries," the research community says it is hard, and the cited Australian group's out-of-sample test supports the research community (TbYgc6_qQzo [06:39] to [07:10]).

**Related** — [[framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers]] (check 6). [[principle--load-gives-risk-context-not-prediction]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[carey-2017-predictive-modelling-of-training-loads-and-injury-in-australian-football]] in the research-paper library; its title matches the paper Ward describes, but this batch did not open it, so verify they are the same study.
